items.prose: A project costs £100 today and pays £30, £40 and £50 at the ends of years 1, 2 and 3. With $v = \tfrac{1}{1 + r}$, its internal rate of return $r$ solves $f(v) = 50v^3 + 40v^2 + 30v - 100 = 0$. Since $f(0.5) < 0 < f(1)$, a safeguarded Newton solver keeps a bracket, starting from $[0.5, 1]$ at $v_0 = 0.5$.

parts.question: Where would a plain Newton step from $v_0 = 0.5$ land? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find $f(0.5)$ and $f'(v) = 150v^2 + 80v + 30$ at 0.5, then take $v_0 - f/f'$.

byKey.sign: You added $f/f'$ instead of taking it away. With $f(0.5)$ negative, the step moves right.

explain.text: $f(0.5) = 6.25 + 10 + 15 - 100 = -68.75$ and $f'(0.5) = 37.5 + 40 + 30 = 107.5$. Newton moves to $0.5 + 68.75/107.5 \approx 1.1395$. The curve is much flatter at 0.5 than near the root, so the tangent overshoots the whole bracket.

parts.question: The landing point 1.1395 from part 1 lies outside $[0.5, 1]$, so the solver takes the bracket's midpoint instead. What is $f$ at the point it tries? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The midpoint of $[0.5, 1]$ is 0.75; put it into $f$.

byKey.accepted: That is $f(1.1395)$. A safeguarded solver never evaluates outside its bracket; it falls back to the midpoint.
byKey.endpoint: That is $f(1)$, as if the step were cut back to the end. The fallback is the midpoint, 0.75.
byKey.sign: Check the sign: $f(0.75)$ sits below zero, like $f(0.5)$, because 0.75 is still left of the root.

explain.text: The fallback is a bisection step, to $v = 0.75$. There $f(0.75) \approx -33.91 < 0$, the same sign as at 0.5, so the bracket shrinks to $[0.75, 1]$. Each step either halves the bracket or lands inside it, which is why the method cannot run away.

parts.question: Using $f(0.75) = -33.90625$ from part 2, the bracket is now $[0.75, 1]$. Take a Newton step from 0.75. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $f'(0.75) = 174.375$, so the step goes to $0.75 + \tfrac{33.90625}{174.375} = 0.75 + \tfrac{7}{36} \approx 0.9444$, inside the bracket.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find $f'(0.75)$, then take $0.75 - f(0.75)/f'(0.75)$.

byKey.sign: You moved left. $f(0.75)$ is negative and $f$ rises, so the root lies to the right.

explain.text: $f'(0.75) = 84.375 + 60 + 30 = 174.375$. The step is $33.90625/174.375 = \tfrac{7}{36}$, so $v = \tfrac{17}{18} \approx 0.9444$. This lands inside $[0.75, 1]$, so the solver keeps it, and $f(0.9444) > 0$ shrinks the bracket to $[0.75, 0.9444]$.

parts.question: From $v = 0.9444$ (part 3) the error is about 0.026, and Newton's errors now obey $e_{k+1} \approx Ce_k^2$ with $C = \tfrac{f''}{2f'} \approx 0.77$ near the root. How many more Newton steps bring the error below $10^{-12}$? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply $e \to 0.77e^2$ again and again, starting from 0.026.

byKey.one-short: After two steps the error is about $2 \times 10^{-7}$, still above $10^{-12}$. One more takes it to about $10^{-14}$.
byKey.bisect: That is how many halvings shrink $[0.75, 0.9444]$ below $10^{-12}$. Newton squares the error each step instead.

explain.text: Each step roughly squares the error and scales it by 0.77: $0.026 \to 5.2 \times 10^{-4} \to 2.1 \times 10^{-7} \to 3.4 \times 10^{-14}$. Real Newton steps give $5.1 \times 10^{-4}$, $2.0 \times 10^{-7}$ and $3.2 \times 10^{-14}$. So 3 steps suffice, and the third beats the target by a factor of about 30.

parts.question: After the three steps of part 4, $v$ has settled. What is the project's internal rate of return $r$? Give a percentage to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Iterate Newton from 0.9444 to find $v^*$, then undo $v = \tfrac{1}{1 + r}$.

byKey.one-minus: You took $r = 1 - v^*$. From $v = \tfrac{1}{1 + r}$, the rate is $\tfrac{1}{v^*} - 1$.

explain.text: Newton from 0.9444 gives 0.918819, then 0.918305, and stays there. So $r = 1/0.918305 - 1 \approx 0.0890$, an IRR of 8.90%. The bracket guarded the start; the quadratic rate finished the job.

items.prose: A desk's curve of at-the-money implied vols, in vol points, holds one cubic piece on $[1, 2]$ years: $p(t) = 16 + 4.2(t - 1) - 0.6(t - 1)^3$. It has $p''(1) = 0$, as a natural spline's first piece must. A 3-year quote of 20.4 arrives, and a junior quant extends the curve without touching $p$. On $[2, 3]$ they fit a cubic $q$ that matches the value, slope and curvature of $p$ at 2 years and passes through 20.4 at 3 years.

parts.question: What is the curvature $p''(2)$ where the two pieces join? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate $p$ twice, then put in $t = 2$.

byKey.sign: The cubic term carries a minus sign, so the curve bends down: $p''(2) = -3.6$.
byKey.slope: 2.4 is the slope $p'(2)$. Curvature needs the second derivative.
byKey.once: You differentiated $(t - 1)^3$ only once. Twice gives $6(t - 1)$, so the coefficient is $-0.6 \times 6 = -3.6$.

explain.text: Two derivatives of $-0.6(t - 1)^3$ give $-3.6(t - 1)$, and the linear term drops out. At the join $t = 2$ that is $-3.6$. The piece bends down as the quotes level off.

parts.question: Using $p''(2) = -3.6$ from part 1, with $p(2) = 19.6$ and $p'(2) = 2.4$, write $q(t) = 19.6 + 2.4u + \tfrac12p''(2)u^2 + cu^3$ with $u = t - 2$. Which $c$ puts $q$ through 20.4 at 3 years? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $u = 1$ into $q$ and set it equal to 20.4.

byKey.no-half: You used $p''(2)$ itself as the $u^2$ coefficient. The form halves it, to $-1.8$.
byKey.sign: The $u^2$ term is $\tfrac12(-3.6) = -1.8$, which you added as $+1.8$.
byKey.once: That follows from $p''(2) = -1.8$, the slip of part 1. With $-3.6$ the $u^2$ term is $-1.8$ and $c = 0.2$.

explain.text: Matching value, slope and curvature fixes three of the cubic's four coefficients. The new quote sets the fourth: $c = 20.4 - 19.6 - 2.4 + 1.8 = 0.2$. So $q(t) = 19.6 + 2.4u - 1.8u^2 + 0.2u^3$.

parts.question: Using $c = 0.2$ from part 2, what is the curvature $q''(3)$ at the far end of the curve? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate $q$ twice in $u$, then put in $u = 1$.

byKey.sign: The end curvature is still negative: $-3.6 + 1.2 = -2.4$. The curve keeps bending down.
byKey.natural: A natural spline would have 0 there, but nothing in the extension asks for it. Compute $q''$ itself.
byKey.once: You differentiated $cu^3$ only once. Twice gives $6cu$, so the end term is 1.2.
byKey.no-half: That uses $c = 2$, the slip of part 2. With $c = 0.2$ the end curvature is $-2.4$.

explain.text: $q''(u) = -3.6 + 1.2u$ rises only to $-2.4$ at 3 years, not to 0. So the extended curve is not a natural spline. A natural spline through all three quotes needs zero curvature at both ends, so it would change $p$ too.

parts.question: Using $q(t) = 19.6 + 2.4u - 1.8u^2 + 0.2u^3$ from part 2, the slope $q'$ turns negative before 3 years, so the curve has a peak. Take one Newton step on $q'(t) = 0$ from $t = 2.75$. Give years to 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Newton on $q'$ steps by $-\tfrac{q'(u)}{q''(u)}$, with $q''(u) = -3.6 + 1.2u$.

byKey.sign: You stepped the wrong way. $q'(2.75)$ is still positive, so the peak lies to the right.
byKey.end-curv: You divided by $-3.6$, the curvature at 2 years. At 2.75 it is $q''(0.75) = -2.7$.

explain.text: To find a peak, Newton solves $q'(u) = 0$, so $q''$ plays the part of the slope. From $u = 0.75$ the step is $0.0375/2.7 = 0.013889$. The exact peak is at $u = 3 - \sqrt5 \approx 0.763932$, so one step, to $t = 2.763889$, lands within $5 \times 10^{-5}$ of it.

parts.question: Using the peak at $t = 2.7639$ from part 4, by how much does $q$ rise above the 3-year quote of 20.4 there? Give vol points to 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $u = 0.7639$ into $q$ and subtract 20.4.

byKey.peak: That is the peak itself. The question asks how far it sits above 20.4.
byKey.start: That is $q$ at 2.75, the starting guess. At the Newton point 2.7639 the rise is 0.0721.
byKey.sign: That uses 2.7361, the wrong-way step of part 4. The peak lies at 2.7639.

explain.text: The quotes only rise, yet the extended curve climbs 0.0721 vol points above 20.4 and then falls back. An error in the peak's place costs only its square in height, so one Newton step is enough. A natural spline refitted through all three quotes rises all the way to 3 years.

items.prose: A credit desk has a borrower's survival probabilities at three dates: $Q(1) = 0.98$, $Q(3) = 0.92$ and $Q(5) = 0.84$. It joins them with the quadratic $p(t)$ through the three points and wants the time when $p(t) = 0.90$. Its model bounds $|Q'''(t)|$ by 0.0006 on $[1, 5]$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Build $p$ from the three Lagrange terms, or test a trial quadratic at all three dates, then put in $t = 4$.

byKey.linear: 0.88 is the straight line between 3 and 5. The quadratic bends, so it sits above the chord there.

explain.text: The slopes between neighbouring points are $-0.03$ and $-0.04$ a year. Their difference, spread over the 4 years between the outer dates, is $\tfrac{-0.04 + 0.03}{4} = -0.0025$, the coefficient of $(t - 1)(t - 3)$. So $p(t) = 0.98 - 0.03(t - 1) - 0.0025(t - 1)(t - 3)$, which fits all three dates, and $p(4) = 0.98 - 0.09 - 0.0075 = 0.8825$.

parts.question: Using $p(4) = 0.8825$ from part 1, take a secant step through $(3, p(3))$ and $(4, p(4))$ towards $p(t) = 0.90$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The chord falls 0.0375 over the year, and we need a fall of 0.02, so $t = 3 + \tfrac{0.02}{0.0375} \approx 3.5333$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find where the line through $(3, 0.92)$ and $(4, 0.8825)$ reaches 0.90.

byKey.linear: That uses $p(4) = 0.88$, the straight-line slip of part 1. With 0.8825 the chord is flatter.

explain.text: The secant replaces $p$ by its chord between 3 and 4, of slope $-0.0375$. Falling from 0.92 to 0.90 takes $\tfrac{0.02}{0.0375} \approx 0.5333$ years. So $t \approx 3.5333$.

parts.question: Using $t = 3.5333$ from part 2, take one Newton step on $p(t) - 0.90$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $p(3.5333) \approx 0.9006235$ and $p'(3.5333) \approx -0.037667$, so the step adds about 0.016553 and $t \approx 3.5499$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $p'(t) = -0.03 - 0.0025(2t - 4)$ and step by $-\tfrac{p(t) - 0.90}{p'(t)}$.

byKey.sign: You stepped back. $p(3.5333)$ is still above 0.90 and $p$ is falling, so $t$ must grow.

explain.text: At 3.5333 the quadratic is 0.0006235 above the target and falls at 0.037667 a year. Newton adds $0.0006235/0.037667 \approx 0.016553$, giving 3.5499. The exact crossing, $-4 + \sqrt{57} \approx 3.54983$, is within $2 \times 10^{-5}$ of it.

parts.question: Using $t^* = 3.5499$ from part 3, bound $|Q(t^*) - p(t^*)|$ by the interpolation error formula with $|Q'''| \le 0.0006$. Give the bound times $10^4$ to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Three points give $\tfrac{Q'''(\xi)}{3!}$ times the product of $t^* - t_k$ over the three dates.

byKey.no-factorial: You left out the $3!$. The error carries $\tfrac{Q'''}{3!}$, so divide by 6.
byKey.fourth: You divided by $4!$. Three points leave a third-derivative term, over $3! = 6$.

explain.text: With three points the error is $\tfrac{Q'''(\xi)}{6}(t - 1)(t - 3)(t - 5)$. At $t^* \approx 3.5499$ the product has size about 2.033, and $\tfrac{0.0006}{6} = 10^{-4}$. So $p$ may be off by up to about $2.03 \times 10^{-4}$ there.

parts.question: Using the bound $2.033 \times 10^{-4}$ from part 4 and the slope $p'(t^*) \approx -0.03775$, how far can the true crossing date lie from $t^*$? Give days to 2 decimal places, with 365 days a year.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A level error $\Delta Q$ moves a crossing by about $\tfrac{\Delta Q}{|p'(t^*)|}$ in time.

byKey.p-at-3: You used the slope at 3 years, 0.035. The crossing is at 3.5499, where the curve is steeper.
byKey.no-slope: You turned the probability error straight into days. Divide by the slope to convert it to time first.

explain.text: Near the crossing $p$ falls 0.03775 a year, so an error of $2.033 \times 10^{-4}$ in level shifts the date by about $0.00539$ years. That is $0.00539 \times 365 \approx 1.97$ days. The root finder's own error, under $10^{-4}$ years, is far smaller than the interpolation's.
